justification:
Round 2 re-check. Both round-1 blocking findings are genuinely fixed, not just reworded, and a fresh full read of the whole article (grown from 20/14 to 31/22 run-code blocks) turned up only one new, minor sourcing nit.

**Fix 1 verified — boxing-cost benchmark.** The `box-cost` block (lines 90-137) no longer re-runs value-types-vs-reference-types.md's 'What a million boxes cost' demo (List<int> vs List<object>, summing and timing). It now benchmarks Hashtable vs Dictionary<int,int> — a structurally different program (two object slots boxed per entry, key and value, instead of one per list element) with its own `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()` allocation-byte measurement, which was exactly the more-rigorous element round 1 asked for instead of wall-clock-only timing. Immediately before the block, the article explicitly builds on the prerequisite rather than re-deriving it: '[Value types vs. reference types](/csharp-dotnet/value-types-vs-reference-types/#what-a-million-boxes-cost) measures that cost once, for a `List<object>` that boxes each *element* it stores. A non-generic dictionary pays the same tax twice over...'. I checked the anchor against the live heading ('### What a million boxes cost' at value-types-vs-reference-types.md:539) — it resolves correctly, and the framing ('measures that cost once... pays the same tax twice over') is an accurate, non-repetitive characterization of what the prior article actually showed, not a hand-wave. This reads as a callback that extends the prior measurement to a new, harder case (double boxing in dictionaries), exactly what the round-1 fix asked for.

**Fix 2 verified — generic-math demo.** The `generic-math` block (lines 528-548) no longer duplicates interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md's exercise solution (`static T Total<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T> { T sum = T.Zero; foreach (var v in values) sum += v; return sum; }`). It is now a `Clamped<T>` method built on `T.Clamp(v, min, max)`, and the follow-on exercise uses `T.CreateChecked(100)` to convert an int literal into T. Both are different INumber<T>/INumberBase<T> members than Zero/`+=`, and the prose earns the change: it explicitly argues what INumber<T> reaches that a hand-rolled interface (an invented `IClampable<T>`) structurally cannot — 'a type you don't own can never be retrofitted to implement an interface you invent after the fact' — and separately explains that Clamp ships a working default implementation (`virtual`, not `abstract`, with `ArgumentException` argument checking) that a hand-rolled `IComparable<T>` clamp would have to write itself. The crosslink to interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md was removed entirely rather than kept and repurposed — grepped the file, zero remaining references to that article or to the old Sum/`IAddable<TSelf>` pattern. Given the demo no longer overlaps, removing the link (rather than forcing an artificial 'see also') is the right call; nothing is left dangling.

**Exercises (new since round 1, 4 total, 3-6 satisfied).** Genuinely varied in form: 'Explain the error' (why `new()` must be last), 'Predict it' (does reification see through a record struct), 'Find the bug' (a covariant indexer that won't compile), 'Extend it' (percentage-of-total entirely in T). Checked each for answer-leakage per the editorial brief's binding pilot lesson: the predict-it stub (`reflect-stub`, lines 322-336) shows no output panel before its solution — only a comment ('// What does each report entry say?') — so a reader cannot see the answer without opening the solution; the extend-it stub (`percent-stub`) is a genuine TODO with no worked output shown either. The explain-the-error and find-the-bug exercises legitimately show the compiler error up front (that is the puzzle, not the leaked answer), consistent with how the article's non-exercise `error=` blocks work throughout. No exercise repeats another exercise's shape, and none opens with 'Predict the...' (the brief's specific 'vary the ending' complaint).

**Fresh full read, one new minor finding.** `INumberBase<TSelf>.Zero Property` is still listed in front matter (line 37-40) but is never cited inline anywhere in the body — grepped the full URL against the article text, it appears exactly once (the front-matter entry itself). This is a leftover from the round-1 Sum/`T.Zero` demo: the prose still says '`T.Clamp(v, min, max)` resolves at compile time... the same way `T.Zero` would' (line 550), but that's an unlinked, uncited mention, and the Zero source was never wired to it or removed. Per the editorial brief's binding rule 3, 'a source in the list that is never cited inline... is a finding.' It's a leftover-cleanup nit, not a fabrication or a duplication problem, and easy to fix either way (add the inline link to the `T.Zero` mention, or drop the source from front matter since Zero is no longer demonstrated).

**Everything else checked and clean.** No filler openings/closings, no restated-title intro, no boilerplate headings. No keyword stuffing. Every other front-matter source (generics overview x2, constraints page, both covariance pages, generic-math overview, Clamp, CreateChecked, Java erasure) is cited inline at least once — spot-checked counts by grepping each URL. No ad code, no policy problems. The two new sections (Hashtable/Dictionary boxing, Clamp/CreateChecked) read as original worked demonstrations, not filler padding added just to grow the block count — each earns its place with a claim the prior sibling article didn't already make. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/generics.md` passes: PASS, blocks=31, executed=22, matching the expected count for this round.
